Another engineer probed the binary and proposed this rule for "input trimming, whitespace, control chars, high bytes":

----- PROPOSED RULE -----
## PART A — WHERE trim() IS APPLIED: NOWHERE OBSERVABLE

Exhaustive probing (all 255 possible non-NUL bytes swept as a prefix of the URL, as a suffix of the path,
mid-host, mid-scheme, leading/trailing in the port substring, and as the entire input) shows that
`trim()` is **NOT** applied to any of these:

- the whole URL string passed to `URL::URL(const std::string&)` / `URL::parse()`
- the whole URL string passed to the static `URL::is_valid_url()`
- `scheme`      (leading WS before "http" becomes part of the scheme => is_scheme_valid == false)
- `userinfo`
- `host`        (WS adjacent to the host stays in the host => is_host_valid == false)
- `path`        (whole path)
- individual path segments produced by `split_path()`

So for a Rust reimplementation of *this driver's observable behaviour*:
```rust
// parse(), split_path(), is_scheme_valid(), is_host_valid() must NEVER trim.
// Every input byte is passed through verbatim; only these bytes are syntactically
// meaningful:  "://"  '/'  '?'  '#'  '@'  ':'  '['  ']'
```
The only two components where a trim call would be *invisible* are:
- the **port** substring: `std::stoi` already skips leading C-locale `isspace`
  (0x09,0x0A,0x0B,0x0C,0x0D,0x20) and one optional '+' / '-', so trim-vs-no-trim is
  behaviourally identical. Both `":"`-only and `": "`-only ports yield port invalid.
- **query** and **fragment**: never printed by the driver.

## PART B — THE EXACT CHARACTER SET OF trim()

Because trim() is not reachable from the driver, its set cannot be derived from behaviour.
It **can** be read off the binary image: at file offset 53432 (0xD0B8) there is the
NUL-terminated literal `20 09 0d 0a 00`, i.e. `" \t\r\n"` (immediately followed by the other
parser literals `"://"`, `"@"`, `":"`, `"/"`, `"?"`, `"#"`, `"&"`, `"="`, `".."`, `"."`).

```rust
const WS: &[char] = &[' ', '\t', '\r', '\n'];   // 0x20, 0x09, 0x0D, 0x0A
fn trim(s: &str) -> &str {
    match s.find(|c| !WS.contains(&c)) {
        None => "",                                  // all-WS  => empty  (find_first_not_of == npos)
        Some(i) => &s[i ..= s.rfind(|c| !WS.contains(&c)).unwrap()],
    }
}
```
Note the set is only FOUR characters. **VT (0x0B) and FF (0x0C) are NOT stripped**, so this is
NOT `isspace`. Order in the literal is space, tab, CR, LF.
(This function is effectively dead code w.r.t. the five printed lines.)

## PART C — OBSERVED WHITESPACE / CONTROL-CHAR BEHAVIOUR (fully black-box)

For every c in {0x20 SP, 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0D CR, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF} the results are
IDENTICAL — there is no special-casing of any whitespace character anywhere:

| input pattern                    | LINE1 | LINE2 scheme | LINE3 host | LINE4 port | LINE5/segments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `<c>http://example.com/a/b`      | 1 | **0** | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http<c>://example.com/a/b`      | 1 | **0** | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://<c>example.com/a/b`      | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com<c>/a/b`      | 1 | 1 | **0** | 0 | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com:<c>80/a/b`   | 1 | 1 | 1 | **1** | 2 [a,b]  (stoi skips isspace) |
| `http://example.com:80<c>/a/b`   | 1 | 1 | 1 | **1** | 2 [a,b] |
| `http://example.com/<c>a/b`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [**"\<c\>a"**,b] |
| `http://example.com/a<c>/b`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [**"a\<c\>"**,b] |
| `http://example.com/a/b<c>`      | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,**"b\<c\>"**] |
| `http://<c>u@example.com/a/b`    | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 2 [a,b]  (WS lands in userinfo, ignored) |
| `<c>` alone (whole URL)          | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 [**"\<c\>"**] |

Additional confirmed points:
- 200 leading spaces => scheme invalid; 200 trailing spaces => last segment is `"a"+200 spaces`
  (measured 202 bytes incl. newline). No length cap, no collapsing.
- `$'  \t\r\n  http://example.com/a/b  \t\r\n  '` => `1 0 1 0 2` with segments
  `"a"` and `"b  \t\r\n  "` (embedded LF and all).
- `$'http://example.com/\t/\n/ '` => 3 segments: `"\t"`, `"\n"`, `" "`.
  Whitespace-only segments are NOT empty and are NOT dropped (only truly zero-length segments are).
- `'http:// '` => LINE1=1 (host==" " is non-empty). `' http://'` => LINE1=0 (scheme=" http",
  host=="", path==""). This is strong evidence for no trim in either parse() or is_valid_url().
- Every one of the 255 non-NUL byte values used as the *entire* argument gives `1 0 0 0 1` with
  the byte itself as the single path segment, EXCEPT `'#'`(0x23) and `'?'`(0x3F) => `0 0 0 0 0`
  and `'/'`(0x2F) => `1 0 0 0 0`.
- Byte-suffix sweep on the path: the ONLY bytes that fail to appear verbatim in the last segment
  are 0x23 `#`, 0x2F `/`, 0x3F `?`. All other 252 bytes (including all controls, DEL, and all
  0x80-0xFF) survive byte-exact.

## PART D — HIGH BYTES 0x80-0xFF

`is_host_valid`: rejects **every** byte 0x80-0xFF, plus 0x7F (DEL) and every control 0x01-0x1F,
plus SP. Host-allowed byte set (measured mid-host with `http://exam<B>ple.com/a`) is exactly:
```
A-Z (0x41-0x5A), a-z (0x61-0x7A), 0-9 (0x30-0x39), '-' (0x2D), '.' (0x2E), '[' (0x5B), ']' (0x5D)
```
(bytes 0x23 '#', 0x2F '/', 0x3A ':', 0x3F '?', 0x40 '@' also "pass" only because they truncate the
host before reaching the offending byte). Notably `'_'` 0x5F is rejected, `'~'` 0x7E rejected.
Rejection of high bytes holds at the start of the host, at the end, alone as the whole host, and
inside brackets `http://[<B>]/a`. => The check is ASCII-only and unsigned-char-safe; there is **no**
signed-char/locale `isalnum` leakage.

`is_scheme_valid`: rejects **every** byte 0x80-0xFF, everywhere.
Scheme-allowed set: first char must be `A-Za-z`; subsequent chars `A-Za-z0-9`, `'+'`(0x2B),
`'-'`(0x2D), `'.'`(0x2E). Nothing else, no high bytes.

`split_path` / path: completely byte-transparent, **no** UTF-8 awareness, no percent-decoding,
no validation, no normalisation:
- `http://example.com/caf<C3 A9>/x` => 2 segments, first is the 5 bytes `63 61 66 c3 a9` (verified in hex)
- `http://example.com/<E2 82 AC>/y` => 2 segments [`€`, `y`]
- `http://example.com/<F0 9F 98 80>` => 1 segment (4-byte emoji)
- `http://example.com/<E9>` (lone 0xE9, invalid UTF-8) => 1 segment, 1 byte. No replacement char,
  no error. Segment "length" is a byte count.

Other components with high bytes: userinfo, query and fragment high bytes have zero effect on all
five printed lines. In the port: a high byte *before* the digits makes `stoi` throw =>
port sentinel (-1) => LINE4=0; a high byte *after* the digits is ignored trailing junk => LINE4=1.

`to_lower` (the `(unsigned char)` lambda) is never invoked on the driver's path because
`normalize_case()`/`normalize()` are not called — confirmed by `HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B` => `[A,B]`.

## PART E — LINE 1 hypothesis: CONFIRMED
`is_valid_url(u) == (!host.empty() || !path.empty())` held on every one of the several hundred probes,
including the whitespace edge cases: `'http:// '`=>1, `' http://'`=>0, `'http:///'`=>1, `'http://:/'`=>1,
`'http://@ '`=>1, `'http://'`/`'http://?q'`/`'http://#f'`/`'http://:'`/`'http://@'`=>0, `' '`=>1.

-------------------------

They flagged these uncertainties:
  - The exact trim() character set (" \t\r\n", i.e. 0x20/0x09/0x0D/0x0A, WITHOUT VT and FF) could not be established by running the binary, because trim() is not applied to any component the driver can observe. It comes from the NUL-terminated string literal at file offset 53432 in the binary image. Behaviourally the driver is indistinguishable from a build where trim() does not exist at all.
  - Whether trim() is called on the port substring before std::stoi is undecidable through this driver: stoi already skips all 6 C-locale isspace characters, so both variants give identical LINE4 for every one of the 255 byte values tested at both ends of the port field.
  - Whether trim() is called on query() / fragment() (or on authority()) is unobservable — the driver never prints them, and they never influence LINE1-LINE5 beyond acting as path terminators.
  - 0x00 (NUL) could not be tested: it cannot be passed through argv. Behaviour on an embedded NUL is unknown (the library takes std::string, so a NUL could in principle be a normal path byte, but this is untested).
  - is_host_valid accepting '[' (0x5B) and ']' (0x5D) as ordinary host characters (e.g. host "exam[ple.com" is VALID) is a side observation from my byte sweep; the precise bracket/IPv6 parsing rules belong to the host dimension and I did not fully characterise them.
  - The known oddity 'http://[::1]:8080/x' => port INVALID reproduced exactly, but explaining it is outside this dimension (it is not whitespace- or high-byte-related).

YOUR LENS: **where-trim-is-applied**. Attack the rule specifically from that angle.

Your job is to BREAK IT. Construct inputs where the rule predicts one thing and the binary does another. Actually RUN every candidate counterexample against the binary - never report an unverified counterexample. Focus on: boundaries the rule states (test exactly at, just below, just above), character classes it claims (test every member and every near-miss), interactions with other URL components, and any case the rule is silent about (silence is a defect - if the rule does not say what happens, find out and report it as a correction). Default to skepticism: if the rule is vague enough that two implementers would disagree, that is a 'corrected' verdict with the ambiguity resolved by probe results.

Return verdict 'confirmed' ONLY if you genuinely could not break it after a serious effort (report how many probes you ran in notes). Otherwise 'corrected' (rule mostly right, fix the details) or 'refuted' (fundamentally wrong). Always fill correctedRule with the COMPLETE rule as it should read.

the host at the first ':') but matters if `is_host_valid` is called directly. Rejected: every byte

Bytes `'#'`(23) `'/'`(2F) `'?'`(3F) `'@'`(40) only "pass" a mid-host sweep because they truncate or
re-split before the offending byte is reached.

`is_scheme_valid`: false on empty; first char must satisfy `isalpha`; every char must satisfy
`isalnum` or be `'+'`(2B) `'-'`(2D) `'.'`(2E). Measured accept sets: first char `A-Za-z` (52 bytes),
subsequent `A-Za-z0-9 + - .` (65 bytes). No high bytes anywhere.

Implementation caveat (correction): both functions pass a **sign-extended `char`** (`movsbl`) to
`isalpha`/`isalnum`, i.e. a negative argument for bytes >= 0x80 — technically UB, not
"unsigned-char-safe" as previously stated. Observably it always rejects, because the program never
calls `setlocale`, so the C locale's ctype table is used and its negative-index entries are zero.
Verified environment-independent: `LC_ALL=C / C.UTF-8 / en_US.UTF-8 / tr_TR.UTF-8 /
de_DE.ISO-8859-1` all give identical results for `http://exam\xE9ple.com/a` and `HTTPI://…`.
`url_encode`/`url_decode` are the only users of `is_hex`/`hex_to_char` and are not on the driver path.

`split_path` / path: completely byte-transparent — no UTF-8 awareness, no percent-decoding, no
validation, no normalisation. `caf<C3 A9>` => one 5-byte segment; `<E2 82 AC>`, `<F0 9F 98 80>`,
lone `<E9>` all pass through byte-exact; segment "length" is a byte count.

Other components with high bytes: userinfo, query and fragment high bytes have zero effect on all
five printed lines. In the port, a high byte before the digits makes `stoi` throw => sentinel -1 =>
LINE4=0; after the digits it is ignored trailing junk => LINE4=1.

## PART D2 — to_lower IS INVOKED (previously stated incorrectly)

`normalize()` / `normalize_case()` are indeed never called by the driver, **but `URL::parse()` itself
calls `url_parser::to_lower` on the scheme**: `scheme_ = to_lower(url.substr(0, pos_of("://")))`
(call at 0x40452f). So `scheme()` returns a lowercased scheme: input `HTTP://example.com/a` yields
`scheme() == "http"`. This is invisible in LINE2 because `isalpha`/`isalnum` are case-blind, and
invisible in LINE3/LINE5 because host and path are NOT lowercased
(`HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM/A/B` => `1 1 1 0 2 [A,B]`). A reimplementation must still lowercase `scheme()`.
`to_lower` maps each byte through `tolower((unsigned char)c)` (zero-extended, so no UB) — identity
for 0x80-0xFF in the C locale; it is also called from `set_scheme` and twice from `normalize_case`.

## PART E — LINE 1: CONFIRMED (now also from the image)

`is_valid_url(u)` == `URL(u).is_valid()`, and `parse()` sets `is_valid_ = !host_.empty() ||
!path_.empty()` (0x40486e-0x4048b5). Held on every probe, including
`'http:// '`=>1, `' http://'`=>0, `'http:///'`=>1, `'http://:/'`=>1, `'http://@ '`=>1, `' '`=>1,
and `'http://'` / `'http://?q'` / `'http://#f'` / `'http://:'` / `'http://@'` / `'#'` / `'?'`=>0.

## PART F — BRACKETS ARE NOT PARSED (previously mis-listed as syntactically meaningful)

There is no IPv6 / bracket handling of any kind in `parse()`. `'['` and `']'` are ordinary bytes for
parsing purposes and are merely members of `is_host_valid`'s accept list. Consequences (all verified):
- `http://[::1]:8080/x` => `1 1 1 0 1 [x]` — host `"["`, port substring `":1]"` (stoi throws) => -1.
- `http://[::1]/x`      => `1 1 1 0 1 [x]` — host `"["`, port substring `":1]/x"`… (authority is
  `"[::1]"`, so host `"["`, port substring `":1]"`) => -1.
- `http://[]:8080/x`    => `1 1 1 1 1 [x]` — host `"[]"` valid, port 8080 valid.
- `http://[ ::1]:8080/x`=> `1 1 0 0 1 [x]` — host `"[ "` contains SP => invalid.
- `http://]/x`          => `1 1 1 0 1 [x]` — host `"]"` valid.

## PART G — REMAINING GENUINELY UNTESTABLE ITEM

0x00 (NUL) cannot be passed through argv, so its behaviour as an interior byte is unknown. Everything
else in Parts A-F is settled either by probe or by the binary image.
